strengths: The paper clearly identifies and motivates two real limitations of prior 3DGS-based language-field registration methods (spatial ambiguity from overlapping Gaussians, and multi-level semantic ambiguity from hierarchical SAM-based pooling), and proposes a coherent solution combining an explicit sparse-voxel geometry with dense AM-RADIO features.

Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks (LERF 3D/2D object retrieval, ScanNet point-cloud understanding) with substantial improvements over recent baselines such as Dr. Splat and OpenGaussian, including large margins on the challenging ScanNet 19-class setting.

Detailed ablation study (Table 4/6) that reasonably disentangles the contributions of geometric regularization (depth/normal supervision), TSDF confidence weighting, RADIO dense features, sliding-window upsampling, and the SCRA/SCGA self-correction modules.

Practical efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated: feature lifting and preprocessing times are drastically reduced relative to distillation-based (LangSplat, OpenGaussian) and registration-based (Dr. Splat) baselines, with reported memory-bottleneck mitigation versus Dr. Splat's reported 256GB RAM requirement.

Extensive qualitative analysis (spillover reduction, small-object segmentation, part-whole disambiguation) and supplementary experiments (autonomous driving on KITTI-360, 3D scene editing, PCA feature visualizations) that broaden the demonstrated applicability of the method.
The multi-level TSDF mesh fusion strategy for combining coarse completeness and fine detail is a sensible and lightweight technical contribution with negligible runtime overhead (~5s).
weaknesses: ProFuse is presented in the related work as the most directly comparable prior method (addressing similar spatial-ambiguity issues via masked context aggregation), yet it is never included as a quantitative baseline in any of the main experiments (Tables 1–3, 5, 7), leaving an important comparison gap.

The method is largely an integration of existing components (SVRaster, patch-wise depth loss from DNGaussian, normal loss from MonoSDF, AM-RADIO, and SCRA/SCGA from RADSeg) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the paper's novelty should be more explicitly framed as a systems/engineering contribution rather than implying each piece is original.

In Table 2 (2D retrieval), LangSplatV2 actually achieves a higher average mIoU (59.88% vs 56.84%) than LESV, and LESV underperforms notably on waldo_kitchen (46.24 vs 59.10 mIoU); the text's characterization as 'highly comparable' or the selective highlighting of the ramen scene understates this shortfall without adequate explanation.

The custom evaluation protocol (normalized cosine similarity thresholds tailored to AM-RADIO's distribution) raises reproducibility and fairness concerns, since it is unclear whether this adaptation is applied identically and without bias across all compared methods using different backbones.

The autonomous-driving (KITTI-360) and scene-editing demonstrations are purely qualitative with no quantitative metrics, limiting the strength of the generalization claims made in the supplementary material.

Some claimed advantages (e.g., the 'refrigerator' example where the method allegedly shows superior fine-grained decoupling but is penalized by coarse ground truth) rely on anecdotal, single-example justification rather than systematic analysis.

Multiple recent/concurrent works this paper heavily depends upon (ProFuse, RADSeg, AnyUp, GAGS) are dated within months of the submission, making it hard to assess true independent contribution versus incremental combination of contemporaneous techniques.
Minor presentation issues remain, such as a broken figure reference ('Figure ??') and no reported variance/multiple-seed results for the quantitative benchmarks.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper crisply identifies two concrete limitations of 3DGS-based language fields (spatial ambiguity from overlapping unstructured Gaussians, and multi-level semantic ambiguity from hierarchical mask pooling) and designs targeted solutions for each.

The core idea of using SVRaster's explicit, disjoint voxel geometry to enable deterministic, geometry-aware feature registration (rather than probabilistic alpha-blending) is a sensible and well-executed design choice that plausibly explains the reported reduction in semantic bleeding/spillover.

Strong and consistent empirical gains on 3D object retrieval (LERF) and point cloud understanding (ScanNet), with large margins over the strongest registration baseline (Dr. Splat), across multiple class granularities.

Substantial and practically important efficiency improvements (roughly 8x reduction in preprocessing time and much faster feature lifting), with a plausible engineering explanation via scalable batch fusion enabled by the disjoint voxel structure.

Thorough ablation study (Table 4) that isolates the contribution of each component (depth/normal supervision, TSDF confidence, raw RADIO features, sliding window, SCRA/SCGA), giving good insight into why the full pipeline is needed.

Good breadth of qualitative analysis, including PCA feature visualizations, multi-level query behavior (bear/bear-nose/bear-legs), and additional out-of-domain demonstrations (KITTI-360 driving scenes, 3D scene editing) that support generalizability claims.

Reasonable attribution of individual techniques to prior work (DNGaussian-style patch depth loss, MonoSDF-style normal loss, RADSeg attention modules), which aids reproducibility understanding of the pipeline.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely an integration of existing components (SVRaster, AM-RADIO's dense alignment, DNGaussian/MonoSDF-style geometric losses, and RADSeg's SCRA/SCGA modules) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the ablation shows that a substantial fraction of the final performance (mIoU jump from 49.79 to 56.11) comes from directly adopting the SCRA/SCGA modules from a concurrent/contemporaneous paper (RADSeg), which somewhat limits the paper's independent methodological novelty.

Several key baselines/techniques the paper builds on (RADSeg, AnyUp, ProFuse) appear to be very recent or concurrent works (e.g., arXiv IDs and workshop dates suggesting late-2025/2026 releases), raising questions about how much of the reported advantage is attributable to the paper's own contribution versus borrowing very recent building blocks; this also makes independent verification/reproducibility harder given the fast-moving baselines.

On the 2D object retrieval benchmark (Table 2), LESV is not uniformly state-of-the-art — it underperforms LangSplatV2 on figurines, teatime, and waldo_kitchen mIoU, and is only roughly on par overall — yet the abstract/conclusion broadly claim SoTA across 2D/3D benchmarks, which slightly overstates the 2D results.

Some qualitative claims are cherry-picked or self-serving (e.g., the 'refrigerator' example is explicitly acknowledged to be penalized by the benchmark's coarse GT, yet is still presented as evidence of superiority), which slightly weakens the rigor of the qualitative argument.

Limited analysis of failure cases or limitations of the proposed method itself (e.g., how the confidence-gating and multi-level TSDF fusion behave in highly cluttered, thin-structure, or textureless scenes) — the main paper lacks a dedicated limitations discussion, with most extended qualitative material relegated to demonstrations rather than critical failure analysis.

The efficiency comparison (Table 5) is reported for a single representative scene (~300 images), without variance across scene scale/complexity, and memory usage (a stated motivation for moving away from 3DGS) is not quantitatively reported for LESV itself, only asserted qualitatively as O(1) memory.

Reported results appear to be single-run numbers without variance/confidence intervals, which is a minor but relevant reproducibility concern given the relatively large performance gaps claimed over baselines.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: clearly articulates two concrete limitations of 3DGS-based language field methods (spatial ambiguity from overlapping Gaussians, and multi-level semantic ambiguity from mask pooling) and designs targeted solutions for each.

Strong quantitative results on ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud understanding, with very large margins over the strongest baseline (+20% mIoU across 19/15/10-class splits), suggesting the structured voxel + dense-feature approach is genuinely effective for this task.

Careful disentanglement ablations (Tables 4 and 5) that separate the contribution of the geometric representation (SVRaster vs 3DGS) from the feature backbone (CLIP vs AM-RADIO), which is good scientific practice and substantiates that gains are not merely from a better encoder.

Practical efficiency gains are compelling and well-documented: substantially lower peak memory (~25GB vs >256GB for Dr. Splat) and much faster preprocessing/feature-lifting time, which matters for real-world deployment.

Extensive supplementary material, including an ablation on feature-upsampling strategies (showing naive deep upsamplers hurt zero-shot retrieval), multi-level TSDF mesh fusion algorithm details, and additional real-world demonstrations (KITTI-360 driving scenes and voxel-level scene editing), which strengthen the applied contribution.
Honest and specific limitations section (feature resolution cap, lack of real-time rendering) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an engineering integration of existing components (SVRaster, AM-RADIO, MonoSDF-style normal/depth losses, DNGaussian-style patch depth loss, RADSeg's SCRA/SCGA upsampling correction) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the novelty lies mainly in the combination and application to language-field registration.

Results are not uniformly state-of-the-art despite the framing: on LERF 3D retrieval LESV is second-best in average mIoU (behind LaGa multi-level) and notably worse than Dr. Splat on the waldo_kitchen scene (43.84 vs 52.00 mIoU); on 2D retrieval/localization LESV trails dedicated 2D methods (Occam's LGS, LangSplat-v2) in mIoU, and on the figurines scene LESV's 3D retrieval mIoU (55.87) is below Dr. Splat's (61.73). The abstract/teaser claim of a "new state-of-the-art across diverse 2D and 3D benchmarks" is therefore somewhat overstated relative to the mixed per-scene/task results.

Baseline comparisons partly rely on the authors' own re-implementation/optimization of Dr. Splat (for memory) and re-implementation of LangSplat/LaGa under a modified protocol, which introduces potential for implementation bias that is difficult for reviewers to independently verify.

The acknowledged effective feature resolution cap (~256) is a significant practical limitation for small/densely packed objects, and this limitation directly explains some of the weaker per-scene results (e.g., figurines), somewhat undercutting the paper's central claims about resolving fine-grained semantic ambiguity.

Several qualitative claims (e.g., 'fine-grained semantic decoupling' on the refrigerator query) are presented as strengths while simultaneously being described as being penalized by ground-truth annotations, making them difficult to verify or benchmark objectively.
Hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., kernel bandwidths β, σ, confidence thresholds) is not analyzed, leaving open questions about robustness and tuning effort across scenes/datasets.
No variance/multiple-run statistics or significance testing are reported for the main benchmark results, limiting confidence in the precision of the reported margins.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper cleanly separates two concrete failure modes of prior 3DGS-based language fields (spatial ambiguity from unstructured/overlapping Gaussians, and multi-level semantic ambiguity from mask-pooled features), and designs targeted solutions for each.

Technically sound combination of an explicit, disjoint Sparse Voxel Rasterization backbone with monocular depth/normal regularization and multi-level TSDF-based confidence gating for deterministic feature registration, replacing probabilistic alpha-blended fusion used by 3DGS methods.

Novel and well-justified exploitation of AM-RADIO's emergent dense patch-token language alignment to obtain multi-scale semantic queries in a single pass, avoiding costly hierarchical SAM-mask training used by LangSplat-style pipelines.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple axes: 3D object retrieval (LERF), 2D localization/retrieval, ScanNet-19/15/10 and ScanNet200 point-cloud understanding, plus efficiency (memory/time) comparisons and informative ablations that disentangle geometry vs. feature-backbone contributions (Tables 4-5).

Commendable scientific transparency: the supplementary honestly reports a negative result showing that a learned deep upsampler (AnyUp) underperforms the proposed sliding-window strategy, rather than only presenting favorable comparisons.

Strong practical/efficiency case: large reductions in preprocessing and feature-lifting time and peak memory relative to Dr. Splat and mask-pooling pipelines, which is meaningful for scalability to dense/large scenes.
Additional qualitative demonstrations (KITTI-360 driving scenes, 3D scene editing via SH manipulation) suggest reasonable generality beyond the primary indoor benchmarks.
weaknesses: The paper's headline claim of establishing state-of-the-art "across diverse 2D and 3D benchmarks" is only partially supported: on LERF 2D retrieval mIoU and on 3D retrieval mIoU vs. LaGa (multi-level), LESV is second-best rather than best, and the framing in the abstract/intro could be tempered to match the more nuanced, competitive-but-not-uniformly-best results shown in Tables 1-2.

The contribution is primarily an integration of existing components (SVRaster, AM-RADIO, RADSeg's SCRA/SCGA, MonoSDF-style normal loss, DNGaussian-style patch depth loss, TSDF fusion) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical idea; the paper would benefit from more explicit discussion of what is genuinely novel versus adapted from cited prior work.

Some evaluation protocol choices are adapted or newly introduced by the authors themselves (e.g., normalized cosine similarity across differing feature distributions, the ProFuse feature-transfer adaptation for ScanNet, and re-implementations of baselines), which, while explained, could introduce subtle biases favoring the proposed method; independent verification or sensitivity analysis would strengthen confidence.

Several key hyperparameters (kernel bandwidth β, confidence decay σ, TSDF blending quantile/temperature) are introduced without sensitivity analysis, raising reproducibility concerns about how tuned these values are per scene/dataset.

Hardware/compute reporting is vague ("equivalent to an NVIDIA RTX 5090"), and no variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for the quantitative benchmarks, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains.

The acknowledged resolution bottleneck (~256 effective feature resolution) meaningfully hurts performance on small/densely packed objects (e.g., figurines scene), which is a non-trivial limitation for a method whose main selling point is fine-grained, deterministic localization.

The method does not support real-time rendering into novel views, unlike the 3DGS-based competitors it is compared against, limiting applicability in interactive/rendering-centric use cases even though it excels at direct 3D queries.
